stem: A bookshop designs a relational database with a Customer table, a Book table and an Order table. In the Customer table, what does a single row represent?

choices.text: One relationship that links the Customer table to the Order table through a matching value.
One instance of the customer entity, holding all of the recorded data for a single customer.
One data type that the database allows in the table, such as text, integer or date values.
One attribute that is recorded for every customer, such as the email address of each person.

stem: A Customer table has a MiddleName column. Many customers have no middle name, or the company does not know it. How should the column be defined so these customers can still be stored?

choices.text: Define the column as NOT NULL so the database stores an empty text string whenever no value is supplied.
Define the column as the primary key so the database fills in a unique value for each row that has none.
Define the column as nullable so rows can be saved with no value, which the database records as NULL.
Define the column as a foreign key so the missing value is looked up from a related table automatically.

stem: A sales spreadsheet stores "Jane Smith, 42 Oak St Seattle" in one cell and the price "9.99 USD" as text. The team moves it into a relational table with a separate column for each attribute. Which TWO benefits does this give? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Each value can be constrained to a suitable data type, such as decimal for prices and integer for quantities.
The table no longer needs a primary key, because every column now holds just one separate piece of data.
The database stops needing data types at all, because one value per column is already clear to every reader.
Queries can easily filter on a single attribute, such as finding only the customers who live in Seattle.
The table can store a different set of columns for each row, so every customer keeps only the fields it uses.

stem: An Employee table has an EmployeeID column. Every employee gets a different EmployeeID, and the database must reject any row that repeats an existing ID or leaves it empty. What is EmployeeID?

choices.text: An index, because it holds a sorted copy of the column with pointers back to the table rows.
A foreign key, because it stores a value that refers to a row in another table of the database.
A primary key, because it uniquely identifies each row and can't hold duplicate or NULL values.
A view, because it presents a virtual table built from the results of a SELECT query on the data.

stem: An Order table must record which customer placed each order, and customer details such as the address are stored only in a Customer table whose primary key is ID. What should the Order table contain?

choices.text: A second primary key that combines the order number with the customer's name, so both stay unique together.
A copy of the customer's name and address columns in every order row, so each order can be read on its own.
A view named Customer inside the Order table that lists the customer's details for each order number.
A CustomerID column defined as a foreign key that holds the ID of the related row in the Customer table.

stem: In an OrderLine table, OrderNo alone repeats for each item on an order and ItemNo alone repeats across orders, but each OrderNo and ItemNo pair occurs only once. How can each line be uniquely identified?

choices.text: Define a composite primary key on OrderNo and ItemNo, because their combination is unique for every line.
Define an index on OrderNo only, because a sorted index makes every value of the column unique by itself.
Define two separate primary keys, one on OrderNo and one on ItemNo, so each column is checked on its own.
Define a foreign key from ItemNo to OrderNo, because linking the two columns makes every line distinct.

stem: An app tries to insert an order with CustomerID 950, but no customer with ID 950 exists. The database rejects the insert. Which relational feature caused this?

choices.text: Normalization, which blocks any row that would duplicate data already held in a different table of the database.
Referential integrity from a foreign key, which requires the value to match an existing primary key row.
An index on the CustomerID column, which refuses values that are not already present in its sorted copy of data.
A NOT NULL constraint on the CustomerID column, which requires that every new order supplies a customer value.

stem: A company tracks sales in one spreadsheet where the customer's address is repeated on every sale. When a customer moves, staff must edit dozens of rows and sometimes miss some. How does a normalized relational design fix this?

choices.text: It adds an index on the address column so every repeated copy of the address can be found and edited together.
It creates a view over the spreadsheet so the address shown in each row can be edited in one place at once.
It keeps all data in one wide table but makes the address column NOT NULL so no row can be missed by staff.
It stores the address once in a Customer table, and orders reference that row, so a move changes a single row.

stem: A junior developer reads that a schema should be normalized. Which TWO are practical rules of normalization? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Use foreign key columns to link related entities, such as an order to the customer that placed it.
Combine related attributes, such as name and address, into one column so each row stays shorter.
Keep a copy of each customer's details on every order so that each order row can be read on its own.
Store every entity in one shared table so that no join is ever needed to read the related data.
Separate each entity, such as customers and products, into its own table in the database schema.

stem: A developer writes a script with the statements CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE. To which group of SQL statements do these belong?

choices.text: Transaction control statements, which commit or roll back a group of changes as one unit of database work.
Data Definition Language (DDL), which creates, modifies and removes tables and other database objects.
Data Manipulation Language (DML), which reads rows from tables and adds, changes or removes those rows.
Data Control Language (DCL), which grants, denies or revokes permissions on objects for users and groups.

stem: A database administrator must let a reporting user named user1 read and add rows in the Product table without changing any table design. Which statement fits?

choices.text: `ALTER TABLE Product ADD user1 VARCHAR(20);`, adding the user to the table so it can read and insert rows.
`INSERT INTO Product (user1) VALUES ('SELECT');`, storing the user's allowed actions as a row in the table.
`GRANT SELECT, INSERT ON Product TO user1;`, giving the user permission to read and add rows in the table.
`CREATE VIEW user1 AS SELECT * FROM Product;`, creating a view named after the user that it can edit freely.

stem: Last month a DBA granted user2 permission to update the Price table. That access is no longer needed, and the DBA wants simply to remove the earlier grant. Which DCL statement does this?

choices.text: `DROP`, which removes a permission from the database permanently so it can't be granted to any user again later.
`DENY`, which removes a permission that was given earlier and returns the user to having no explicit permission.
`REVOKE`, which removes a permission that was previously granted so the user no longer has it on that table.
`DELETE`, which removes the stored permission row for the user from the table the permission was granted on.

stem: Which TWO statements belong to Data Manipulation Language (DML), the group that works with the rows stored in tables? (Select TWO)

choices.text: `UPDATE`, which modifies the data in rows that already exist in a table, usually matched by a WHERE clause.
`GRANT`, which gives a user or group the permission to perform specific actions on a database object.
`CREATE`, which adds a new object to the database, such as a table, a view or a stored procedure.
`ALTER`, which modifies the structure of an existing table, for example by adding a new column to the table.
`INSERT`, which adds new rows to a table, with a list of values for the columns named in the statement.

stem: A developer meant to change the address of customer 1 and ran `UPDATE Customer SET Address = '123 High St.';`. Now every customer has that address. What caused this?

choices.text: The Address column was defined as NOT NULL, so the database copied the new value into every row of the table.
The statement used UPDATE instead of ALTER, and only ALTER can change the value of a single row in a table.
The Customer table had no index on the Address column, so the change was applied to the whole table instead.
The statement had no WHERE clause, so UPDATE applied the new value to every row in the Customer table.

stem: A Promotions table holds last year's offers. The team wants to remove all of its rows but keep the table, with its columns and keys, ready for new offers. Which statement fits?

choices.text: `REVOKE SELECT ON Promotions;`, which hides every existing row so that only newly inserted rows are visible.
`DELETE FROM Promotions;`, which removes every row of data while the table itself stays in the database.
`DROP TABLE Promotions;`, which empties the table's rows while keeping the column definitions for reuse.
`ALTER TABLE Promotions;`, which resets the table to its original empty state with the same set of columns.

stem: An existing Product table needs a new Weight column. The table already holds thousands of rows that must be kept. Which type of statement should the developer run?

choices.text: A `CREATE TABLE` statement, a DDL statement that adds the column by defining the Product table a second time.
An `ALTER TABLE` statement, a DDL statement that modifies the structure of the existing table to add the column.
An `INSERT` statement, a DML statement that adds the Weight column by inserting a row that holds its name.
An `UPDATE` statement, a DML statement that adds the new column to every existing row along with a value.

stem: A report runs `SELECT FirstName, LastName FROM Customer WHERE City = 'Seattle';`. Users complain the names come back in a different order on different days. What should be added?

choices.text: A `GROUP BY LastName` clause, which keeps rows in the order they were first inserted into the Customer table.
An index on the City column, which makes the database always return rows sorted by the indexed column value.
A primary key on the LastName column, which forces the table to store and return rows sorted by last name.
An `ORDER BY LastName` clause, which sorts the returned rows by the LastName column every time it runs.

stem: An Order table has a CustomerID foreign key and a Customer table holds addresses under the primary key ID. A query must list each order number with its customer's city. What should the query use?

choices.text: A `UNION` that stacks the rows of the Order table on top of the Customer table, matched by the column order.
An `ALTER TABLE` that adds a City column to Order, so the query can read the city from one table only.
A `JOIN` that matches Order.CustomerID with Customer.ID, so each order row is combined with its customer row.
A `GRANT` that lets the Order table read the Customer table, so the city appears in the order rows directly.

stem: A marketing list must show every customer, including customers who have never placed an order. Orders that exist should appear beside each customer. Which join gives this result?

choices.text: A left outer join from Customer to Order, which keeps every customer and shows NULL where no order matches.
An inner join from Order to Customer, which returns every order and adds the customers who have no orders.
An inner join from Customer to Order, which returns all customers and fills in orders where they exist.
A cross join between Customer and Order, which pairs each customer only with the orders that customer placed.

stem: Analysts often need order numbers with each customer's name and delivery address, which requires joining the Order and Customer tables. The DBA wants to give them one object they can query like a table. What should the DBA create?

choices.text: An index on the Order and Customer tables, which stores the joined columns so analysts can query the index.
A view defined by a SELECT that joins Order and Customer, which analysts can query and filter like a table.
A foreign key between Order and Customer, which lets analysts read both tables as one combined table.
A new table that copies the joined order and customer data, refreshed by hand whenever an analyst asks.

stem: Several applications rename products by running the same UPDATE logic with a product ID and a new name. The team wants that logic kept inside the database and run on command with parameters. Which object fits?

choices.text: A view, which stores a SELECT query and lets applications pass a product ID to update the matching row.
An index, which keeps a sorted copy of the Name column so applications can change product names faster.
A stored procedure, which holds SQL statements with parameters that applications run on command with EXEC.
A foreign key, which links each product row to its new name stored in a separate table of product names.

stem: A Product table has millions of rows, and a search page runs `SELECT * FROM Product WHERE Name = @name;` many times a minute. Each query scans the whole table and is slow. What should be added?

choices.text: An index on the Name column, so the database can find matching rows without reading every row.
A foreign key on the Name column, so the database links each name to the matching product row.
A view on the Product table that selects the Name column, so the search page reads fewer rows.
A stored procedure that runs the SELECT, so the database caches the full Product table in memory.

stem: To speed up reports, a developer added indexes on almost every column of a busy Orders table. Reports are faster, but inserting and updating orders is now slower. Which TWO explain this? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Indexes lock the table as read-only until the database rebuilds them each night, so changes wait in a queue.
Indexes make the foreign keys on the table check every row of the related tables before each new insert.
Indexes turn the Orders table into a view, so every insert must first run the view's SELECT statement again.
Each index stores its own sorted copy of column data, so many indexes consume extra storage space as well.
Each index must be maintained whenever rows are inserted, updated or deleted, which adds work to every change.

stem: A team lead lists facts about primary keys in SQL Server and Azure SQL Database for new hires. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The columns of a primary key can't contain NULL, because every row must be identifiable by its key value.
A primary key is required on every table, and the database refuses to create a table that is defined without one.
A table can have several primary key constraints, one for each column that holds unique values in the table.
Primary key values may repeat across rows as long as at least one other column in the row is different.
The database enforces uniqueness of a primary key by automatically creating a unique index on its columns.

stem: Which statement correctly describes the difference between a view and an index in a relational database?

choices.text: A view stores a full copy of a table's rows for faster reads; an index is a saved query that combines tables.
A view is a virtual table based on a SELECT query; an index is a sorted copy of column data used to find rows fast.
A view runs parameterized SQL logic on command; an index links rows in one table to rows in another table.
A view grants permissions to users on selected rows; an index removes rows that are no longer needed by queries.

stem: A team uses Azure SQL Database and also an Azure Database for PostgreSQL server. A new developer asks why the procedural code for each looks slightly different. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Only Azure SQL Database supports SQL; PostgreSQL uses its own query language that is unrelated to the SQL standard.
Both systems use PL/SQL exactly, and the differences come only from the editor tools the developers have chosen.
Each system uses its own SQL dialect; Azure SQL Database uses Transact-SQL, and PostgreSQL uses PL/pgSQL.
Azure SQL Database uses PL/pgSQL and PostgreSQL uses Transact-SQL, so each team must learn the other's dialect.

stem: A developer writes `CREATE TABLE Product (ID INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, Price DECIMAL NULL);`. Which statement about the new table is correct?

choices.text: Name can hold whole numbers only, because VARCHAR stores integer values of up to twenty digits in length.
ID may repeat across rows, because a PRIMARY KEY only sorts the rows and does not enforce any uniqueness.
Price must always have a value, because DECIMAL columns are mandatory in every row of a relational table.
ID uniquely identifies each row, Name is a mandatory text column, and Price may be left empty as NULL.

stem: A startup is building a new cloud-native web application that needs one relational database. The team wants the latest stable SQL Server features and no responsibility for operating systems, patching or backups. Which Azure service fits best?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database as a single database, with its own dedicated resources managed through a logical server.
SQL Server on an Azure virtual machine, installed from a SQL Server image in the Azure Marketplace.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, deployed into a dedicated subnet of the startup's own Azure virtual network.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, running the MySQL Community Edition engine that Azure manages.

stem: A software company sells a SaaS app and gives each of its 300 customers a separate Azure SQL Database. Most databases are idle most of the day, but each one has short, unpredictable peaks. The company wants to cut costs without starving any database at its peak. What should it use?

choices.text: The Business Critical service tier for every database, so that each one keeps a local read-only replica for peaks.
A larger SQL Server VM size, so that all databases run inside one instance whose memory and CPU can be resized.
One SQL Managed Instance, so that all 300 customers share a single database with a tenant ID column in each table.
An elastic pool, so that the databases share a set amount of compute and storage purchased for the whole group.

stem: Which statement correctly describes an Azure SQL Database elastic pool?

choices.text: A collection of SQL Managed Instances in one subnet that share one set of logins, jobs and linked servers.
A set of compute and storage resources shared by several databases on one logical server, billed for the pool.
A cluster of SQL Server virtual machines that together host one very large database split across many nodes.
A group of database copies kept in several Azure regions so that the application can fail over during an outage.

stem: A company runs an on-premises SQL Server instance with 40 databases. The applications use SQL Server Agent jobs, cross-database queries and linked servers. It wants a managed PaaS service and as few application changes as possible. Which service should it choose?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, so that all 40 databases share resources and keep running their Agent jobs.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, which provides full SQL Server compatibility and access to the operating system.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, which provides a SQL Server instance with near-100% compatibility as a managed service.
Azure SQL Database single databases, one per on-premises database, managed together through one logical server.

stem: A manufacturer's SQL Server database works with a vendor monitoring agent that must be installed on the same server as SQL Server and needs access to the operating system. It wants to move to Azure quickly without changing anything. Which option should it use?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it has near-100% compatibility with SQL Server Enterprise Edition features.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because it lets you add extensions that run inside the database.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, because it gives full control of the SQL Server engine and the operating system.
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, because it separates compute and storage and scales to very large databases.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: Which TWO Azure services for SQL Server workloads are platform as a service (PaaS) offerings? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, a fully managed instance with near-100% compatibility.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, a VM image with SQL Server already installed.
Azure Dedicated Host, a physical server reserved for VMs that run the SQL Server engine.
Azure Virtual Machine Scale Sets running SQL Server Express on several identical VMs.
Azure SQL Database, a fully managed database designed for new cloud applications.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: A team moves a database from SQL Server on an Azure VM to Azure SQL Database. Which TWO tasks will Microsoft perform for the team after the move? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Deciding which indexes to create and rewriting slow queries that the application sends to the database.
Applying updates and patches to the database engine and to the operating system underneath it.
Creating database logins and users and granting them permissions on the tables of the database.
Choosing which application data to keep, which to delete and how sensitive each column of data is.
Taking automatic database backups that the team can use for a point-in-time restore when needed.

stem: A developer needs an Azure SQL Database for a test environment that is used for a few hours on some days and sits idle for long periods. She wants compute charges only while the database is in use. Which option fits best?

choices.text: The Hyperscale service tier with read-only geo-replicas, which turn off compute in the primary when idle.
An elastic pool with one database in it, which bills only for the minutes when the database runs queries.
The provisioned compute tier, which keeps a fixed amount of compute allocated and billed every hour of the day.
The serverless compute tier, which scales compute with demand and can pause the database when it is inactive.

stem: In Azure SQL Database, what is the role of the logical server (the SQL Database server) that you create along with your databases?

choices.text: A central administrative point for its databases, holding logins, firewall rules, auditing and failover groups.
A full SQL Server instance with its own SQL Server Agent, Database Mail and linked servers for its databases.
A virtual machine that you sign in to with Remote Desktop to install SQL Server updates for the databases.
A physical host reserved for your company so that no other Azure customer's databases run on the hardware.

stem: Which Azure SQL option gives a database administrator the experience most similar to running SQL Server in the company's own datacenter, including full control of the instance and the operating system?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, deployed into the company's Azure virtual network.
Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, managed through a single logical server.
Azure SQL Database serverless, which scales compute automatically with demand.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, running on Windows Server or Linux VMs.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: A team moved its SQL Server database to a single Azure VM and assumed the VM's availability SLA protected the database. During a SQL Server service crash, the VM stayed up but the database was offline. What explains this?

choices.text: The VM SLA applies only when the database is also registered in an Azure SQL Database elastic pool on the same logical server.
Microsoft restarts SQL Server automatically only on Linux VMs, so the team should have chosen a Linux image for the database.
The VM SLA covers the virtual machines, not the SQL Server processes on them, so database high availability is the team's job.
SQL Server on Azure VMs supports only the Express edition, which has no automatic restart of the database service after a crash.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: An app that will move to Azure uses SQL Server CLR assemblies inside the database. The team prefers a PaaS service so that Microsoft handles patching. Which service supports this with the fewest changes?

choices.text: SQL Server on Azure VMs, because Microsoft patches the operating system and SQL Server for all VM images.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, because CLR modules are among the SQL Server features it supports as a PaaS service.
Azure SQL Database as a single database, because it runs the latest stable SQL Server Enterprise Edition engine.
Azure SQL Database in an elastic pool, because pooled databases can load assemblies from the shared resources.

stem: A bank needs its managed SQL Server databases to use private IP addresses inside its own Azure virtual network, with connectivity to on-premises over ExpressRoute, and it relies on instance-level features. Which service fits best?

choices.text: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines in a public subnet, with the operating system firewall left open to clients.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, which is based on the community edition and offers zone-redundant HA.
Azure SQL Managed Instance, which is deployed with a native virtual network implementation and private IP addresses.
Azure SQL Database single databases, reached from the internet through the logical server's firewall rules.

stem: Which TWO capabilities does SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines offer that Azure SQL Database does not? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Choosing when operating system and SQL Server updates are installed, and installing extra software on the host.
Built-in high availability of the database itself, covered by Microsoft without any extra configuration.
Online changes of compute and storage resources without any downtime for the database during resizing.
Automatic patching of the database engine and operating system by Microsoft with no action from the customer.
Any supported SQL Server version and edition, with full parity with the matching on-premises SQL Server.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: What does the Hyperscale service tier of Azure SQL Database mainly provide?

choices.text: A full SQL Server instance with SQL Server Agent jobs, linked servers and cross-database queries for many databases.
Operating system access on the database host so that monitoring agents and other software can be installed there.
A shared pool of resources for many small databases whose usage peaks happen at different times of the day.
Very large databases with independently scalable compute and storage, plus fast backup and restore regardless of size.

stem: A company owns SQL Server licenses and is moving workloads to Azure SQL Database, Azure SQL Managed Instance and SQL Server on Azure VMs. It wants to use those licenses to lower costs. What should it use?

choices.text: Moving all databases into one elastic pool, which converts the existing licenses into shared pool resources.
The Azure Hybrid Benefit, which gives a discount on SQL Server licensing and is available for all three products.
The serverless compute tier, which removes the SQL Server license fee whenever the database is paused or idle.
Azure reserved VM instances, which discount VM compute in return for a one-year or three-year commitment.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: Before migrating several on-premises SQL Server databases, a company wants to find out which features they use that Azure SQL Database or SQL Managed Instance might not support. What should it do?

choices.text: Create an elastic pool and move the databases into it, because the pool rejects any database with unsupported features.
Run an Azure SQL assessment with Azure Migrate or SQL Server enabled by Azure Arc to evaluate the instances.
Enable auto-pause in the serverless tier, because a paused database reports features it could not load at startup.
Register the on-premises servers with the SQL IaaS Agent extension, which converts unsupported features automatically.

stem: A company runs a LAMP-stack web application (Linux, Apache, MySQL, PHP) on premises. It wants a managed Azure service for the database with automatic backups and patching, and no change to the database engine. Which service should it use?

choices.text: Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because PostgreSQL accepts MySQL dump files without changes.
SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines, running SQL Server on Linux so that the stack stays on a Linux server.
Azure SQL Database, after converting the schema and queries from MySQL to Transact-SQL for the SQL Server engine.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, a fully managed service based on the MySQL Community Edition engine.

stem: A logistics firm's on-premises PostgreSQL database uses PL/pgSQL stored procedures, custom data types and geometric data. It wants a managed Azure service and minimal application refactoring. Which service should it choose?

choices.text: Azure SQL Managed Instance, because it provides near-100% compatibility with on-premises database engines.
Azure Database for MySQL flexible server, because it supports stored procedures and custom server parameters.
Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server, because it runs the community version of the PostgreSQL engine.
Azure SQL Database Hyperscale, because it scales storage independently for large geometric and custom data.

stem: Which TWO capabilities describe PostgreSQL, the engine behind Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Defining custom data types and adding extensions, code modules that queries can run inside the database.
Storing schemaless JSON items that are partitioned automatically across regions for global distribution.
Grouping related columns into column families queried by a SQL-like language of its own, such as CQL.
Keeping all data only in memory as key-value pairs for caching, so it is lost when the server restarts.
Storing and working with geometric data such as lines, circles and polygons in relational tables.

stem: A team uses Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server for a development database that is needed only during working hours. It wants to cut costs at night and on weekends without deleting the server. What should it do?

choices.text: Stop the server when it is not needed, because compute billing stops immediately while the server is stopped.
Move the database into an elastic pool, which bills only for the hours when queries run against the server.
Enable auto-pause in the serverless compute tier, which pauses the server after a configured idle delay.
Set the backup retention to the minimum, because the compute charge is calculated from the backup storage size.

stem: A developer is building a first prototype on Azure Database for MySQL flexible server. The database will see light, irregular use and must cost as little as possible. Which compute tier should she choose?

choices.text: The Memory-Optimized tier, because it gives the most memory per vCore for each connection the app opens.
The General Purpose tier, because it is the only tier that supports automatic backups and point-in-time restore.
The Burstable tier, which is designed for low-cost development and low-concurrency workloads like this one.
The Hyperscale tier, because it separates compute from storage and bills compute only while queries run.

stem: A company runs an important production database on Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. It must stay available if an entire availability zone in the region fails, with no loss of committed data. What should it configure?

choices.text: The Burstable compute tier, which moves the server between zones automatically when it detects a failure.
Read replicas in the same zone, which take over writes automatically whenever the primary server stops responding.
A longer backup retention period, which lets the server restore itself in a new zone without losing any data.
Zone-redundant high availability, which keeps a warm standby in another zone with synchronous replication.

stem: Which TWO statements about Azure Database for MySQL flexible server are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It gives administrators sign-in access to the underlying Linux VM to install their own tools.
It takes automatic backups and supports point-in-time restore for up to 35 days of retention.
It can be added to an Azure SQL Database elastic pool to share compute with other databases.
It is based on the MySQL Enterprise Edition and requires customers to bring their own licenses.
It is based on the MySQL Community Edition and is offered as a fully managed PaaS service.

stem: An online shop uses Azure Database for MySQL flexible server. Patches sometimes require a server restart, and the shop wants these to happen only at its quietest time, early Sunday morning. What should it configure?

choices.text: Manual patching through a remote session to the server, so that the shop installs each update by itself.
A custom maintenance schedule, so that automated patching is applied in the window that the shop chooses.
A read replica in another region, so that patches are applied to the replica instead of the primary server.
The stop and start feature, so that the server skips all patches while it is stopped on Sunday mornings.

stem: A DBA connects pgAdmin to Azure Database for PostgreSQL flexible server. Querying and monitoring work, but she cannot perform a server backup and restore the way she did on the on-premises server. Why?

choices.text: pgAdmin cannot connect to Azure Database for PostgreSQL, so the session is actually running against a local copy.
Backups require the Memory Optimized compute tier, and the server was created in the General Purpose tier.
The server is managed by Microsoft, so some server-focused functions such as server backup and restore are not offered.
The database must first be moved to an Azure SQL Database elastic pool before backup functions become available.

stem: A company is choosing between Azure SQL Database and SQL Server on Azure VMs for a new reporting database. Which statement correctly compares how they keep the SQL Server version current?

choices.text: Azure SQL Database always runs the latest stable engine and is updated by Microsoft; on a VM you choose and install the version and its updates.
Both services let you pick any SQL Server version, but only the VM option applies updates automatically without the customer's action.
SQL Server on a VM always runs the latest engine, while Azure SQL Database stays on the version chosen when the database was created.
Both services are updated by Microsoft on a fixed schedule, and neither allows the customer to choose an older SQL Server version.

services: SQL Server on Azure Virtual Machines

stem: A bank moves $40 from a customer's checking account to her savings account. The debit succeeds, but the server fails before the credit is written. The database undoes the debit so neither balance changes. Which ACID property does this behavior show?

choices.text: Durability, because the database keeps the balances on disk so they survive the server failure and are there after restart.
Consistency, because the database checks that each account balance stays within the allowed overdraft limit for the bank.
Isolation, because other transactions running at the same time cannot see the half-finished transfer between the two accounts.
Atomicity, because the debit and the credit form one unit of work that either completes fully or is rolled back as a whole.

stem: While a transfer between two accounts is in progress, a second query reads both balances. The query must never return one balance from before the transfer and the other from after it. Which ACID property guarantees this?

choices.text: Isolation, which makes sure concurrent transactions cannot interfere with each other or see each other's partial changes.
Consistency, which makes sure that a completed transfer leaves the two balances adding up to the same total as before.
Atomicity, which makes sure the debit and the credit of the transfer are applied together or not applied at all.
Durability, which makes sure the committed balances are written to storage and survive a restart of the database server.

stem: An online store's database confirms to a customer that her order is committed. A moment later the datacenter loses power. When the database comes back, the order is still there. Which ACID property is the reason?

choices.text: Isolation, because the order transaction was kept separate from other customers' orders running at the same time.
Atomicity, because every row of the order was written together as a single unit of work before the power failed.
Durability, because a transaction that has been committed stays committed even if the system is switched off.
Consistency, because the order moved the database from one valid state to another valid state when it was committed.

stem: A team is describing the database behind its point-of-sale system to a new hire. Which TWO characteristics are typical of a transactional (OLTP) workload like this one? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The workload is mostly read-only, and the stored data is refreshed in large loads every night from several source systems.
Data is stored in a highly normalized schema so that each fact is kept once and many small transactions can run independently.
Data is preaggregated across dimensions such as date and region so that summary queries return without scanning detail rows.
The store keeps many years of history so that analysts can compare trends across long periods without touching other systems.
Records are created, read, updated and deleted many times a day, and each change must be available to the application at once.

stem: A ticketing company sells concert seats on its website. Each purchase must reserve a seat, take payment and record the sale, and no seat may ever be sold twice. Which type of data workload is this?

choices.text: A batch workload, because the purchases are collected through the day and processed together in one scheduled job each night.
A data lake workload, because ticket sales arrive from many devices and are kept in their raw format for later exploration.
An analytical workload, because each sale adds rows that later feed reports on how many seats sold for each concert and venue.
A transactional workload, because each purchase is a small unit of work that must be recorded at once with ACID guarantees.

stem: A retail chain's leaders want to see total sales by region, product category and month for the last five years, and compare this year with previous years. Which type of data workload supports this need?

choices.text: A transactional workload with stronger locking, so the five-year totals cannot change while each manager's report query is running.
A transactional workload on the point-of-sale database, querying the live sales tables directly every time a manager opens the report.
A file share workload, exporting each store's daily receipts to a shared folder where managers open and total them in a spreadsheet.
An analytical workload on a read-optimized store that holds historical sales copied from the operational systems at intervals.

stem: Every month-end, finance runs a large report that totals millions of order rows directly on the order-entry database. During the report, customers complain that placing orders becomes very slow. What is the most suitable fix?

choices.text: Remove the ACID guarantees from the order-entry database so that orders no longer wait for locks held by the month-end report.
Ask customers to place orders outside business hours at month-end so that the finance report can use the database without contention.
Copy the order data on a schedule into a separate analytical store such as a data warehouse and run the month-end report there.
Normalize the order tables further so that each order row is smaller and the report reads fewer bytes for every order it adds up.

stem: Sales managers want to see revenue totals by region, then drill down to city and to individual store, and get answers almost instantly. Which part of an analytical solution is designed for this?

choices.text: A normalized transactional database with primary and secondary indexes on every column that a manager is likely to filter on.
An OLAP or semantic model that stores measures preaggregated across dimensions and hierarchies such as region, city and store.
A message queue that delivers every new sale to the managers' devices as it happens so that they can add up the totals themselves.
A data lake folder of raw daily sales files that managers query with their own scripts each time they need a new total.

stem: A manufacturer wants to keep sensor logs, JSON files from its apps, product photos and exports of its ERP tables in one low-cost store. Data scientists will decide later how to use them. Which analytical store fits best?

choices.text: A data lake, which holds large volumes of structured, semi-structured and unstructured data in native format and applies schema on read.
An OLAP semantic model, which stores preaggregated measures across dimensions so that business users get fast summary results.
A data warehouse, which loads only structured and curated data into relational tables whose schema is fixed before data is written.
A transactional database, which stores normalized rows with ACID guarantees so that every change is consistent and durable at once.

stem: A finance department needs consistent, low-latency reports on cleaned sales, budget and cost data that has a well-known structure. Analysts query it daily with SQL. Which analytical store fits this workload best?

choices.text: A key-value store that saves each report result under a key so that analysts can fetch any finished report with a single lookup.
A data lake that keeps every source file in its original format so that each analyst applies a structure when running a query.
A data warehouse that stores the cleaned data in a relational schema optimized for read operations such as reporting queries.
A transactional database that the sales application writes to, so analysts always query the most recent rows as soon as they arrive.

stem: A trainer explains how a data lake differs from a data warehouse. Which TWO statements about a data lake are correct? (Select TWO)

choices.text: It processes every write as an ACID transaction with row-level locking, so it can serve as the system of record for live orders.
It requires every file to match a relational table definition before the file is accepted, an approach called schema on write.
It is limited to small datasets of a few gigabytes because each query must load all of the files into memory on a single server.
It stores data in its native, raw format and applies structure only when the data is read, an approach called schema on read.
It can hold structured tables, semi-structured JSON or logs and unstructured images or video side by side in the same store.

stem: An order-entry database has slowed down because it holds ten years of orders. The company still needs the old orders for trend reports. What is the common approach for transactional systems?

choices.text: Keep a relevant window such as the current fiscal year in the OLTP system and offload older history to a data warehouse.
Copy all ten years of orders into every table of the OLTP database so that each query finds the old data without needing a join.
Delete orders older than the current year from all systems, because historical data has no further value once orders are fulfilled.
Move the entire order-entry application into the data warehouse so that live orders and history are stored in one read-optimized place.

stem: When data is copied from a highly normalized OLTP database into an analytical store, designers often combine some tables and repeat values such as product names in many rows. Why do they do this?

choices.text: To enforce stronger ACID guarantees, because repeated values let the analytical store roll back each load if any of the rows fails.
To make analytical queries perform faster, because fewer joins are needed when related values already sit in the same table.
To make inserts and updates simpler, because changing a product name then only needs to touch a single row in the store.
To save storage space, because repeating a product name in many rows takes less space than storing it once in a separate table.

stem: Which TWO statements correctly describe analytical (OLAP) workloads compared with transactional (OLTP) workloads? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Analytical workloads suit strategic decisions, because their data is typically refreshed at intervals that match business needs.
Analytical workloads are mainly built for the many small insert, update and delete operations that a checkout system performs.
Analytical stores rely on heavy row-level locking so that many small updates from the live application can commit safely.
Analytical stores are refreshed when each business event happens, so they always reflect every change at the moment it occurs.
Analytical stores are usually read-only or read-mostly and hold large volumes of historical data or business metrics.

stem: A retailer runs a nightly job that reads all of the day's sales files, aggregates them and writes summary tables that reports use the next morning. What is the main drawback of this batch approach?

choices.text: The job cannot aggregate data, because batch processing can only copy files from one location to another unchanged.
The job must keep every source file locked for writing all day, so the stores cannot record any sales until it finishes.
The job loses accuracy, because batch processing samples only a small part of each file to finish within its time window.
Results can be several hours old, because the job processes the data only after a whole period has been collected.

stem: Data scientists want to try ad hoc questions against large raw files in the company's data lake, adjust their code and see results within a session, using Python. Which kind of analytical work is this?

choices.text: A scheduled batch report that a data engineer runs once a month and publishes to business users as a fixed set of summary tables.
A transactional workload, because each query the data scientists run is a small unit of work that must be committed with ACID guarantees.
Interactive data exploration, for example in notebooks such as Jupyter on Azure Databricks or Microsoft Fabric over the data lake.
A preaggregated dashboard that business users open to view fixed totals by region without writing or changing any queries.

stem: A company's order application runs on Azure SQL Database. Managers also want simple near-real-time reports run directly against that same operational database instead of a separate copy. What is this combined workload called?

choices.text: Online analytical processing (OLAP), because the reports read and aggregate data that the operational system has already stored.
Hybrid transactional and analytical processing (HTAP), because one system handles both transactions and analytical reporting.
Batch processing, because the reports collect the orders over the day and process them together in a single scheduled run.
Extract, transform and load (ETL), because the reports first copy the order data and then reshape it before showing results.

stem: A bank's account-opening application must create a customer record, an account record and a first deposit as one operation, and refuse any account without a valid customer. Which workload type and store fit best?

choices.text: An analytical workload in a data lake, storing each request as a raw JSON file and validating the customer later when the file is read.
A transactional workload in a relational database that enforces ACID transactions and integrity rules between the related records.
An analytical workload in a semantic model, preaggregating new accounts by branch so that managers can see daily totals quickly.
A batch workload that collects the day's account requests and loads them all into a data warehouse during the overnight run.

stem: A new sales application needs read access to the customer database, and a departing contractor's sign-in must lose all permissions on it. Which data role is typically responsible for these tasks?

choices.text: A database administrator, who manages the security of the data in the database and grants or denies users access.
An AI engineer, who integrates large language models and machine learning features into applications and workflows.
A data engineer, who builds and monitors the pipelines that move and transform data between systems for analysis.
A data analyst, who explores the data to find trends and builds reports and visualizations that the sales team uses.

stem: A company's operational database must be recoverable after a storage failure or a user deleting rows by mistake. Who typically designs and tests the backup and restore plan?

choices.text: The data engineer, because data engineers own all copies of data that move between systems across the organization.
The data analyst, because analysts know which tables matter most for the reports that the business relies on each day.
The database administrator, because DBAs work with stakeholders on backup and recovery plans for the database systems.
The data scientist, because data scientists build the models that predict when storage hardware is likely to fail.

stem: A company wants data from its CRM, its ERP database and web log files combined every night, cleaned and loaded into an analytical store. Which role typically designs and builds this?

choices.text: A database administrator, who maintains the CRM and ERP databases and makes sure they are backed up and perform consistently.
A business user, who reads the dashboards built on the analytical store and makes decisions about sales and operations.
A data analyst, who explores the loaded data, finds trends and builds the reports and visualizations that leaders use.
A data engineer, who designs and implements ingestion pipelines, cleansing and transformation, and analytical data stores.

stem: The sales director wants an interactive report that shows which products are trending in each region, built from the curated data already in the data warehouse. Which role typically builds it?

choices.text: A data analyst, who explores data to identify trends and relationships and builds reports and visualizations.
A database administrator, who tunes the warehouse's performance and grants users permission to read its tables.
A data engineer, who builds the pipelines that move, clean and load the source data into the data warehouse.
An AI engineer, who builds AI-powered features in applications using large language models and data sources.

stem: Overnight data loads into the warehouse have started finishing late, and some mornings a load fails without anyone noticing until reports show old numbers. Whose responsibility is it to manage and monitor these loads?

choices.text: The business users, because they decide which reports are important and should check that the figures look right each day.
The data analyst, because analysts are the first people to see the old numbers when they open their reports each morning.
The database administrator of the source system, because the source database is where the data that is being loaded is stored.
The data engineer, because data engineers own the management and monitoring of data pipelines so loads perform as expected.

stem: Queries on the company's order database have become slow at peak times, and the database must stay available around the clock. Which role is typically responsible for the database's performance and availability?

choices.text: The data analyst, who designs the reports that query the order data and decides which visuals each report should show.
The database administrator, who is responsible for availability, consistent performance and optimization of databases.
The AI engineer, who adds large language model features to the order application so customers can ask questions in chat.
The data engineer, who builds the pipelines that copy order data into the analytical store for reporting each night.

stem: Priya provisions a new Azure SQL Database for an order application, and later builds a process that copies its order data into the data warehouse every night. Which roles is she performing in these two tasks?

choices.text: Database administrator for both tasks, because both tasks change the database and so must be done by its administrator.
Data analyst for the provisioning, because she chose the database, and data engineer for the copy, because it supports reporting.
Database administrator for the provisioning, and data engineer for the pipeline that transfers data to the data warehouse.
Data engineer for both tasks, because provisioning a database and copying data between systems are both data infrastructure work.

stem: A hiring manager is writing a job description for a database administrator. Which TWO responsibilities belong in it? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Granting or denying users access to the data in the databases and managing the privileges that each account holds.
Exploring data to identify trends and relationships, and publishing reports and visualizations for business decisions.
Building AI-powered chat features over company data by integrating large language models into the applications.
Designing ingestion pipelines that combine data from many systems and load it into an analytical data store each night.
Creating and maintaining backup and recovery plans so the databases can be restored after a disaster or human error.

stem: Which TWO tasks are typical responsibilities of a data engineer? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Granting a new application read permission on the customer tables and removing the access of accounts that are no longer used.
Building an interactive report with charts that lets sales managers compare monthly revenue across regions and products.
Restoring a production database to an earlier point in time after a user accidentally deletes a large number of order rows.
Applying data cleansing routines and transformations so that data from different systems is consistent before it is analyzed.
Implementing pipelines that transfer data between systems and monitoring them so that data loads perform as expected.

stem: A team lead is listing what the company's data analysts are responsible for. Which TWO items belong on the list? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Tuning the operational database's indexes and settings so that peak-hour queries from the application stay fast.
Defining the backup schedule for the production databases and testing restores after hardware or human failures.
Exploring data to identify trends and relationships that answer business questions for the organization's leaders.
Implementing the nightly pipelines that move raw data from the operational systems into the company's data lake.
Designing and building analytical models, and enabling analytics for the business through reports and visualizations.

stem: Customer data moves from on-premises systems through pipelines into several cloud data stores. The company wants privacy maintained across that whole path and governance rules identified for it. Which role is described as responsible?

choices.text: The business user, because business users own the customer relationship and know which details are sensitive for each client.
The data engineer, who ensures data privacy is maintained from on-premises to the cloud data stores and identifies governance rules.
The data analyst, because analysts decide which customer fields appear in each report and who in the business may see them.
The AI engineer, because AI engineers prepare data for language models and so must remove sensitive values before it is used.

stem: Finance reports show different revenue totals from the sales team's reports. Investigation finds that one source sends dates in two formats and duplicates some orders before the data is loaded. Which role should fix the root cause?

choices.text: The database administrator, by restoring the analytical store from last night's backup every morning before the reports run.
The data analyst, by adding a filter to each report so that the duplicate orders are hidden from the visuals that leaders see.
The data engineer, by adding cleansing and transformation steps to the pipeline so the data is standardized and deduplicated.
The business users, by checking each order against the source application and correcting the totals in their own spreadsheets.

stem: A company describes three needs: keep the order database secure and recoverable, move and clean order data into the warehouse, and show leaders monthly order trends. Which mapping of roles to needs is correct?

choices.text: Database administrator for security and recovery, data engineer for moving the data, and data analyst for the trend reports.
Data engineer for security and recovery, database administrator for moving the data, and data analyst for the trend reports.
Database administrator for security and recovery, data analyst for moving the data, and data engineer for the trend reports.
Data analyst for security and recovery, data engineer for moving the data, and database administrator for the trend reports.

stem: Before a data warehouse project, a manager asks who will design the analytical data stores that the reporting will use, such as the warehouse tables the pipelines load. Which role typically owns this design work?

choices.text: The database administrator, who looks after the operational databases and so must design every new analytical store as well.
The data engineer, who designs and implements data stores for analytical workloads as well as the pipelines that load them.
The data analyst, who designs the reports and visuals and so decides how every table in the warehouse is physically stored.
The business user, who requested the reporting project and therefore defines the warehouse's tables and their data types.

stem: A retail company keeps its product list in a table where every product has the same fields: ProductID, Name, Category and Price. Each product is a row and each field is a column. How is this data best described?

choices.text: Unstructured data, because product names are free text that an application has to interpret before it can use them.
Vector data, because each product row is a list of values that can be compared numerically with the other rows.
Semi-structured data, because the fields have names that describe their values, much like the keys in a JSON document.
Structured data, because every record follows the same fixed schema of named fields set out as rows and columns.

stem: An app saves each customer as a JSON document. Most customers have one email address, some have several phone numbers and email addresses, and a few have no contact details at all. Which description fits this data?

choices.text: Binary data, because JSON documents are stored as raw bytes that only the app that wrote them can interpret and render.
Unstructured data, because the number of contact entries differs by customer, so there is no structure at all to rely on.
Semi-structured data, because the documents share a general structure but their fields can vary from one customer to the next.
Structured data, because each document is stored in JSON and JSON always enforces one fixed set of fields per entity.

stem: A law firm stores scanned contract images, recordings of client phone calls and short training videos. None of these files follow a field-and-value layout. How is this content classified?

choices.text: Relational data, because each file can be linked to a client record by storing the client's key next to the file's path.
Unstructured data, because documents, images, audio and video have no specific internal structure of fields and values.
Structured data, because each file has a name, a size and a creation date that are recorded the same way for every file.
Semi-structured data, because the files are grouped into folders by client, which gives the collection a loose hierarchy.

stem: A data team is sorting its sources into structured, semi-structured and unstructured data. Which TWO sources are unstructured data? (Select TWO)

choices.text: An XML feed of supplier prices that uses nested elements and attributes to describe each product.
A CSV export of the order table, with a header row and the same six columns on every line.
JSON messages from a web API in which some optional fields appear only for some of the records.
Audio recordings of support calls that are saved as MP3 files at the end of every conversation.
Photos of damaged goods that customers upload as JPEG files together with their return requests.

stem: Customers are stored in a relational table with a fixed schema. A developer now wants to record a loyalty tier, but only for a few customers. What does the fixed schema mean for this change?

choices.text: A new column must be defined in the table schema, and rows without a loyalty tier simply hold no value in it.
The whole table must be converted to JSON first, because relational tables cannot hold a value that is optional.
The value can be added to just those customer rows, because each row in a table can carry its own extra fields.
The tier must be kept in a separate file, because a relational table's schema cannot change after it is created.

stem: A data model describes customers, products and sales orders. For each customer it records a name, an address and a phone number. In data terms, what are the name, address and phone number?

choices.text: Schemas, because each one defines the full set of fields that every customer record must contain.
Keys, because each one is a value that uniquely identifies a single customer among all the others.
Attributes, because each one is a characteristic that describes an instance of the customer entity.
Entities, because each one is a separate thing that the organization needs to keep track of over time.

stem: A support team wants its search to find articles that mean the same thing as a question, even when they share no words. Its developers convert each article into a list of numbers that represents its meaning. What is this kind of data called?

choices.text: Column-family data, a set of logically related columns that are grouped together and stored in the same family.
Key-value data, in which each number in the list is a key that points to one stored copy of the original article.
Delimited text data, in which every number in the list is separated by a comma and each article ends with a new line.
Vector data (embeddings), a numerical representation of content that AI applications use to find similar content.

stem: Thermostats send JSON readings. After a firmware update, newer devices add a humidity field that older devices never send. A loader that maps every message to a fixed set of table columns now drops the new field. What is the underlying cause?

choices.text: The messages are unstructured data, so no loader can read individual fields from them without first rendering them.
The messages are semi-structured data whose fields vary by device, while the loader assumes one fixed structured schema.
The loader reads the messages as binary large objects, so it ignores any field name that appears after the first record.
JSON can hold only one level of fields, so the humidity value has to travel in a separate message from the temperature.

stem: A supplier sends purchase orders as XML. Each order has elements for the buyer and a list of line items, and some orders also include delivery instructions that others leave out. How should this data be classified?

choices.text: Semi-structured data, because the tags give the orders a structure while the elements can vary per order.
Structured data, because XML tags require every element to appear in every order in one fixed sequence.
Unstructured data, because XML is plain text, and any text without a table layout is unstructured data.
Graph data, because the nested elements of each order form nodes and edges linked to the other orders.

stem: Which TWO statements describe features of semi-structured data? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Records can contain nested values, such as an address object or a list of contact methods.
The data can be kept only in a relational database whose tables reference one another by keys.
The data has no internal organization, so an application must render it to make sense of it.
Every record must contain exactly the same set of fields, in the order the schema defines.
Field names or tags are stored with the values, so each record describes its own structure.

stem: An online store sells TVs, which have a screen size and resolution, and shirts, which have a size, color and fabric. A single fixed table for all products would leave most columns empty in most rows. Which representation suits this catalog best?

choices.text: Unstructured data, saving a photo of each product label so the attributes never need to be recorded as fields at all.
Semi-structured data, such as one JSON document per product holding only the attributes that apply to that product.
Delimited text, writing all products to a CSV file in which each line may have a different number of values on it.
Structured data in one table with a column for every attribute of every product type, as fixed schemas handle variety best.

stem: A media company stores thousands of video files. Editors want to list every video longer than ten minutes without opening the files. What makes this possible while the videos themselves remain unstructured data?

choices.text: Storing the videos in a graph database, because nodes and edges let a query measure the running time of each file.
Converting each video into a CSV file, because delimited text is the only format that data tools can filter by value.
Placing the videos in a relational table as binary columns, so the database can read each video's length from its bytes.
Recording descriptive metadata, such as duration and resolution, as structured fields stored with or beside each file.

stem: An architect lists the kinds of data a new workload will handle. Which grouping matches each kind of data to its category correctly?

choices.text: Structured: JSON and XML files. Semi-structured: relational tables. Unstructured: images and documents.
Structured: key-value data. Semi-structured: images and video. Unstructured: relational tables and JSON.
Structured: relational tables. Semi-structured: JSON, XML and key-value. Unstructured: images and documents.
Structured: relational tables and images. Semi-structured: documents. Unstructured: JSON and XML files.

stem: A finance system exports invoices to a CSV file. The first line names the columns, and every line after it holds the same five values in the same order. A colleague says the data is unstructured because it sits in a text file rather than a database. Which reply is accurate?

choices.text: The data is binary, because the CSV file stores its values as bytes that a spreadsheet must render to display them.
The data is semi-structured, because a CSV file has a header row that describes its fields the way JSON keys do.
The colleague is right, because any data kept in a file instead of a database is classed as unstructured data.
The data is structured, because every row follows the same fixed set of fields; being in a file does not change that.

stem: A payroll team must be sure that every employee record has a salary, a tax code and a bank account, and it runs the same totals over all records every month. Why does structured data suit this better than semi-structured data?

choices.text: Structured data is always smaller on disk than semi-structured data, so the monthly totals finish in less time.
Structured data can be stored only as binary objects, so the payroll values cannot be read without permission.
Structured data has a fixed schema, so every record has the same fields and the totals can rely on them existing.
Structured data lets each record add or omit fields freely, so new payroll fields never need a change to the schema.

stem: A traffic camera saves a JPEG image of each passing car and also sends a JSON record with the time, the speed and the lane, where some records add a field for a flagged violation. How should these two outputs be classified?

choices.text: The JSON records are semi-structured data and the JPEG images are unstructured data.
The JSON records are unstructured data and the JPEG images are semi-structured data.
Both are semi-structured data, because each image and each record carries a time stamp from the camera.
Both are structured data, because the camera produces each image and each record in the same way for every car.

stem: A government agency publishes monthly statistics as a table of rows and columns. The files must open in spreadsheets, scripts and nearly any data tool, and people must be able to read them in a text editor. Which file format fits best?

choices.text: Avro, because its JSON header describes the fields, so any spreadsheet tool can open the binary blocks of records.
Delimited text such as CSV, because it is human-readable plain text that a wide range of tools can read and write.
A binary large object, because raw binary files can be read by any application without a character encoding.
Parquet, because its columnar layout and compression make it the format that every spreadsheet opens directly.

stem: A developer opens a data file in which objects are enclosed in braces, collections in square brackets, and each attribute is written as a name and a value separated by a colon. Which format is this?

choices.text: Apache Avro, a row-based format that stores its records in binary blocks after a header that describes the data.
Comma-separated values (CSV), in which each row is a line of plain text and each field is separated by a comma.
Extensible Markup Language (XML), which wraps every element and attribute in opening and closing angle-bracket tags.
JavaScript Object Notation (JSON), a hierarchical format suited to both structured and semi-structured data.

stem: A manufacturer's older ordering system exchanges data in a human-readable format that wraps every element in angle-bracket tags such as `<Customer>`. Newer partners prefer a less verbose format that has largely replaced it. Which formats are these?

choices.text: The older format is JSON, and the newer, less verbose format that has largely superseded it is XML.
The older format is XML, and the newer, less verbose format that has largely superseded it is JSON.
The older format is CSV, and the newer, less verbose format that has largely superseded it is Parquet.
The older format is Avro, and the newer, less verbose format that has largely superseded it is ORC.

stem: A hospital stores X-ray images, recorded dictation and PDF reports. These files hold raw binary data that applications must interpret and render, rather than text mapped to readable characters. What do data professionals commonly call files like these?

choices.text: Column families, because each file keeps its related bytes together in a named group inside the database.
Delimited files, because each image and recording is split into fields that a separator character divides.
Binary large objects (BLOBs), the term for files such as images, audio and video stored as raw binary data.
Fixed-width files, because each image and recording is stored with a set number of characters per field.

stem: Analysts query a data lake table with 200 columns, but most queries read only four of them over millions of rows. The team wants a compressed, self-describing file format that lets queries skip the columns they do not need. Which format fits best?

choices.text: Parquet, because its columnar layout stores each column's data together, so queries read only the needed columns.
XML, because the tags around every value let the query engine find the four requested columns by element name.
Avro, because its row-based layout keeps every field of a record together, so whole records are read in one pass.
CSV, because plain text with a header row lets the query engine jump straight to the columns that were requested.

stem: A team writes a steady stream of event messages from a message bus to storage, and downstream jobs usually read whole records. It wants a compact binary format whose header describes the schema. Which format fits best?

choices.text: ORC, because its columnar layout lets each new event be appended as one row without rewriting any columns.
Avro, a row-based format with a JSON header that describes the data, suited to write-heavy, whole-record use.
Parquet, because a columnar layout is the best choice when records arrive one after another and are read whole.
XML, because human-readable tags make each event easy to append and keep the storage per message small.

stem: A data engineer needs a file format that stores data by column for read-heavy queries that touch only a few columns. Which TWO formats store data in a columnar layout? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Comma-separated values (CSV)
Extensible Markup Language (XML)
Apache Avro
Optimized Row Columnar (ORC)
Apache Parquet

stem: A team is moving its data lake files from CSV to Avro, Parquet and ORC. Which TWO characteristics do these three optimized formats share? (Select TWO)

choices.text: They are compressed, machine-readable binary formats, so files take less space than the same data as plain text.
They store every record as a set of angle-bracket tags, so nested values can be represented inside each record.
They need a separate schema file deployed next to each data file, because the data files hold no field information.
They are plain-text formats, so anyone can open a file in a text editor and read the values without special tools.
They embed a description of the schema in each file, so the files are self-describing to the tools that read them.

stem: Which TWO workloads are a good fit for a key-value data store, where each value is read and written by its unique key? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Searching the full text of support articles and ranking them by their relevance.
Running monthly reports that join orders, customers and products in many ways.
Keeping web session state that the app looks up by session ID on every request.
Finding friends of friends up to four links away in a social network of users.
Caching product pages so the site can return each one by its page key quickly.

stem: A key-value database treats each stored value as opaque: it can find a value only by its key. How does a document database differ from this basic key-value model?

choices.text: A document database stores tables of rows and columns and divides the columns into groups of logically related columns.
A document database stores entities as nodes and the relationships between them as links that queries can traverse.
A document database stores each value as a JSON document that the system is optimized to parse, index and query by field.
A document database stores only binary files, so the system cannot read any of the fields inside the stored values.

stem: A utility collects readings from millions of smart meters. Rows are wide and sparse, writes arrive constantly, and related columns, such as all voltage readings, are read together. Which type of nonrelational database is designed for this pattern?

choices.text: A column-family database, which groups logically related columns into column families within each row.
A document database, which keeps each meter's readings in one JSON document rewritten after every reading.
A graph database, which stores each meter as a node and each reading as a link to the next reading in time.
A key-value database, which keeps each meter's readings as one opaque value that is replaced on every write.
